## Purpose and main decisions

I cleaned the Case 31 survey data and evaluated two proposed measures. The results support an employee proficiency index; the operational effectiveness items remain separate.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(haven)
library(labelled)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
tab <- function(x, digits = 3) knitr::kable(x, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE)
data_raw <- read_sav("Case 31 Data_efcu_1.sav", user_na = FALSE)
raw_snapshot <- data_raw
```

## Import and inspection

The SPSS file contains **128 rows and 34 columns**: 32 questionnaire items (q3-q27, q30-q34, q37, and q38) and two precomputed variables, `OverallEmployeePerformace` and `employeeperformance`. I excluded both summaries because their calculation is undocumented.

A variable label describes a column, such as savings rates for q7. A value label identifies a response code, such as 1 = Very high.

```{r}
#| label: inspect
tibble(rows = nrow(data_raw), columns = ncol(data_raw)) |> tab()
```

At import, q7 has **10 missing responses (7.8%)**, q8 has **21 (16.4%)**, and q37 has **7 (5.5%)**. Their SPSS missing code 6 becomes NA through `read_sav()`. I did not impute values.

```{r}
#| label: raw-missing
raw_missing <- tibble(variable = names(data_raw),
                      n_missing = map_int(data_raw, ~sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  filter(n_missing > 0) |>
  mutate(percent_missing = 100 * n_missing / nrow(data_raw))
tab(raw_missing, 1)
```

## Data dictionary and measurement levels

Most labels identify the item clearly. However, q8 repeats q9's statement-frequency label, q38's “headquarter” label needs clarification, and the precomputed variables lack labels. I standardized the questionnaire labels.

```{r}
#| label: dictionary-function
dictionary <- function(df) {
  tibble(variable = names(df),
         description = map_chr(df, ~if (is.null(attr(.x,"label"))) "" else attr(.x,"label")),
         class = map_chr(df, ~class(.x)[1]),
         distinct_nonmissing = map_int(df, ~n_distinct(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
         missing = map_int(df, ~sum(is.na(.x))),
         codes = map_chr(df, function(x) {
           z <- attr(x,"labels")
           if(is.null(z)) "" else paste(z, names(z), sep=" = ", collapse="; ")
         }))
}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Original descriptions

```{r}
dictionary(data_raw) |> select(-codes) |> tab()
```

### Original value labels

```{r}
dictionary(data_raw) |> select(variable, codes) |> tab()
```

:::

| Variables | Measurement interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| q11, q12, q27, q38 | Nominal yes/no categories; code 3 is nonresponse, not a third substantive category. |
| q13-q26 | Categorical awareness/use statuses; an ordinal engagement interpretation is explored separately. |
| q9 | Ordered frequency categories, but desirability peaks at “About right,” not at an endpoint. |
| q3-q8, q10, q30-q34, q37 | Ordinal ratings. Agreement items and their justified mean index are treated as approximately interval for the requested alpha, factor analysis, and averaging. Equal intervals remain an assumption. |

q38 is nominal because residence has no numerical ranking. q7 is ordinal because perceived rates are ordered. q3 is an ordinal agreement item, treated as approximately interval for scale analysis. None of these coded responses is a ratio measurement.

Scale directions, awareness/use categories, and missing codes are essential for interpretation. The agreement endpoints are familiar, but I added the unlabeled middle responses (2-4), 3 = Unaware for q13-q26, and 3 = No answer for yes/no items.

## Repair labels and check allowed values

I kept the raw data unchanged and relabeled q8 **Borrowing interest rates**. For q37, the questionnaire calls code 6 “No opinion,” while Exhibit 31.2 calls it “No answer.” Both represent a nonrating and are treated as missing.

```{r}
#| label: repair-labels
data <- data_raw |> select(matches("^q[0-9]+$"))
labels <- c(q3="Employees are courteous", q4="Employees are helpful",
 q5="Employees are professional", q6="Employees are available",
 q7="Savings interest rates", q8="Borrowing interest rates",
 q9="Frequency of account statements", q10="Accuracy of account statements",
 q11="Account statements are understandable", q12="Account information is confidential",
 q13="Regular share accounts", q14="Special subaccounts", q15="Christmas club accounts",
 q16="Individual retirement accounts", q17="Master credit cards", q18="Signature loans",
 q19="New car loans", q20="Late model car loans", q21="Older model car loans",
 q22="Household goods/appliance loans", q23="Recreational loans",
 q24="Share collateralized loans", q25="IRA loans", q26="Line of credit loans",
 q27="Currently has a credit union loan", q30="Credit union loan rates are lower",
 q31="Personnel keep financial information confidential", q32="Loan applications processed promptly",
 q33="Financial services meet member needs", q34="Loan applications are simple to complete",
 q37="Overall management and operation rating", q38="Lives in headquarters area")
var_label(data) <- as.list(labels[names(data)])
agreement <- c("Strongly disagree"=1,"Disagree"=2,"Uncertain"=3,
               "Agree"=4,"Strongly agree"=5)
rate <- c("Very high"=1,"High"=2,"Average"=3,"Low"=4,"Very low"=5,"No opinion"=6)
awareness <- c("Aware and have used"=1,"Aware but have not used"=2,"Unaware"=3)
yesno <- c("Yes"=1,"No"=2,"No answer"=3)
data <- data |> mutate(
 across(c(q3:q6,q30:q34), ~set_value_labels(.x,agreement)),
 across(c(q7,q8), ~set_value_labels(.x,rate)),
 across(q13:q26, ~set_value_labels(.x,awareness)),
 across(c(q11,q12,q27,q38), ~set_value_labels(.x,yesno)),
 q9=set_value_labels(q9,c("Too often"=1,"Very often"=2,"About right"=3,
                         "Not often enough"=4,"Never"=5)),
 q10=set_value_labels(q10,c("Excellent"=1,"Good"=2,"Fair"=3,"Poor"=4)),
 q37=set_value_labels(q37,c("Excellent"=1,"Good"=2,"Average"=3,"Poor"=4,
                          "Very poor"=5,"No opinion / no answer"=6)))
allowed <- setNames(rep(list(1:5),ncol(data)),names(data))
for(n in c("q7","q8","q37")) allowed[[n]] <- 1:6
for(n in c(paste0("q",13:26),"q11","q12","q27","q38")) allowed[[n]] <- 1:3
allowed$q10 <- 1:4
quality <- imap_dfr(data, function(x,n) tibble(
 variable=n, observed=paste(sort(unique(as.numeric(x))),collapse=", "),
 missing=sum(is.na(x)), percent_missing=100*mean(is.na(x)),
 undefined=sum(!is.na(x) & !(x %in% allowed[[n]]))))
tab(quality,1)
stopifnot(all(quality$undefined == 0))
```

All observed values fall within the defined coding ranges. Code 3 in q12 is a nonresponse; code 3 in q13-q26 means Unaware and remains valid.

## Missing responses and reverse coding

I explicitly recoded 6 to NA for q7, q8, and q37, and 3 to NA for yes/no items. This adds **22 missing responses in q12**. I also removed the nonresponse value labels.

```{r}
#| label: clean-missing
data <- data |> mutate(
 across(c(q7,q8,q37), ~remove_value_labels(na_if(.x,6),6)),
 across(c(q11,q12,q27,q38), ~remove_value_labels(na_if(.x,3),3)))
map_dfr(c("q7","q8","q37","q11","q12","q27","q38"),
        ~tibble(variable=.x, missing=sum(is.na(data[[.x]])))) |> tab()
```

I used `6 - original` for q7, q8, and q37, and `5 - original` for q10, keeping the originals. Higher reversed values mean higher savings rates, better statement accuracy, or better overall management. **Higher q8r means higher borrowing rates, which is not necessarily more favorable.**

```{r}
#| label: reverse-ratings
reverse_item <- function(x, maximum, description, value_labels) {
  labelled(maximum + 1 - as.numeric(x), labels=value_labels, label=description)
}
rate_reversed <- c("Very low"=1,"Low"=2,"Average"=3,"High"=4,"Very high"=5)
data$q7r <- reverse_item(data$q7,5,"Savings rates: higher = higher rates",rate_reversed)
data$q8r <- reverse_item(data$q8,5,"Borrowing rates: higher = higher rates",rate_reversed)
data$q10r <- reverse_item(data$q10,4,"Statement accuracy: higher = better",
                         c("Poor"=1,"Fair"=2,"Good"=3,"Excellent"=4))
data$q37r <- reverse_item(data$q37,5,"Overall management: higher = better",
                         c("Very poor"=1,"Poor"=2,"Average"=3,"Good"=4,"Excellent"=5))
data$q9_about_right <- labelled(ifelse(is.na(data$q9),NA_real_,
                                      as.numeric(data$q9 == 3)),
                                c("Other frequency"=0,"About right"=1),
                                label="Account statement frequency is about right")
```

q9 is not reversed because “About right” is the middle response. Instead, `q9_about_right` equals 1 for code 3 and 0 for another valid response, preserving NA. Yes/no items remain categorical.

### Awareness items: categorical interpretation and ordinal exercise

Awareness and use depend on members' needs, so I would summarize each service separately using category frequencies and percentages aware or used, rather than average the 14 items into an attitude index.

For the ordinal exercise, I created q13r-q26r using `4 - original`: 1 = Unaware, 2 = Aware but have not used, and 3 = Aware and have used. This assumes increasing engagement, not equal spacing, and does not justify averaging across products.

```{r}
#| label: awareness-ordinal
for(n in paste0("q",13:26)) {
 data[[paste0(n,"r")]] <- reverse_item(data[[n]],3,
  paste0(var_label(data[[n]]),": ordinal engagement (higher = used)"),
  c("Unaware"=1,"Aware but have not used"=2,"Aware and have used"=3))
}
awareness_summary <- map_dfr(paste0("q",13:26), function(n) {
 x <- as.numeric(data[[n]])
 tibble(service=var_label(data[[n]]),valid=sum(!is.na(x)),
        percent_aware=100*sum(x %in% c(1,2))/sum(!is.na(x)),
        percent_used=100*mean(x == 1,na.rm=TRUE),
        percent_unaware=100*mean(x == 3,na.rm=TRUE))
})
tab(awareness_summary,1)
```

### Verify every transformation

Cross-tabulations confirm the reversed values and missing pairs. Assertions check that missing patterns stay unchanged and complete pairs sum to the required constant.

```{r}
#| label: verify-recodes
reverse_names <- c("q7","q8","q10","q37",paste0("q",13:26))
verification <- map_dfr(reverse_names,function(n) {
 x <- as.numeric(data[[n]]); y <- as.numeric(data[[paste0(n,"r")]])
 total <- if(n == "q10") 5 else if(n %in% paste0("q",13:26)) 4 else 6
 stopifnot(identical(is.na(x),is.na(y)), all((x+y)[!is.na(x)] == total))
 tibble(variable=n,original=x,reversed=y) |> count(variable,original,reversed,name="n")
})
tab(verification)
stopifnot(identical(data_raw,raw_snapshot))
```

## Evaluate candidate multi-item measures

I calculated alpha without automatic reversal and fitted one factor using minimum residual extraction. Both item sets have complete responses from all 128 respondents.

```{r}
#| label: measurement-checks
employee_items <- as.data.frame(lapply(data[paste0("q",3:6)],as.numeric))
operations_items <- as.data.frame(lapply(data[paste0("q",30:34)],as.numeric))
employee_alpha <- psych::alpha(employee_items,check.keys=FALSE)
operations_alpha <- psych::alpha(operations_items,check.keys=FALSE)
employee_fa <- psych::fa(employee_items,nfactors=1,rotate="none",fm="minres")
operations_fa <- psych::fa(operations_items,nfactors=1,rotate="none",fm="minres")
reliability <- tibble(measure=c("Employee proficiency","Operational effectiveness"),
 items=c(4,5),n=c(nrow(employee_items),nrow(operations_items)),
 raw_alpha=c(employee_alpha$total$raw_alpha,operations_alpha$total$raw_alpha),
 variance_explained=c(employee_fa$Vaccounted[2,1],operations_fa$Vaccounted[2,1]),
 RMSR=c(employee_fa$rms,operations_fa$rms))
tab(reliability)
item_evidence <- function(a,f) tibble(item=rownames(a$item.stats),
 r_drop=a$item.stats$r.drop, loading=as.numeric(unclass(f$loadings)[,1]),
 communality=as.numeric(f$communality))
bind_rows(item_evidence(employee_alpha,employee_fa),
          item_evidence(operations_alpha,operations_fa)) |> tab()
```

### Employee proficiency: create the index

**Employee alpha = 0.866**, with corrected item-total correlations of .657-.823 and loadings of .72-.92. The factor explains 63% of variance. Courtesy, helpfulness, professionalism, and availability describe related employee-service qualities on the same positive agreement scale, supporting a mean index.

The index is provisional: one-factor fit is imperfect (chi-square = 12.72, df = 2, p = .0017; TLI = .874; RMSEA = .204). Strong item relationships support its use, but further factor analysis is needed before claiming a single validated construct.

### Operational effectiveness: retain separate items

**Operational alpha = 0.539**, with corrected item-total correlations of .216-.483. All are positive, and the questionnaire contains no reverse-worded item in this set.

Loadings range from .29 to .79, and the factor explains only 23% of variance. Pricing, confidentiality, processing speed, meeting needs, and form simplicity cover different attributes. I kept them separate and would compare their frequencies, medians, and responses by residence or loan status.

## Create and inspect the supported index

The employee index is the mean of q3-q6, requiring at least three valid answers. All 128 respondents answered all four. Scores remain on the 1-5 scale, with higher scores indicating better employee assessments.

```{r}
#| label: employee-index
n_employee <- rowSums(!is.na(employee_items))
index <- rowMeans(employee_items,na.rm=TRUE)
index[n_employee < 3 | is.nan(index)] <- NA_real_
data$employee_proficiency_index <- labelled(index,
 label="Employee proficiency: mean q3-q6 (at least 3 valid); higher = better")
tibble(valid=sum(!is.na(index)),missing=sum(is.na(index)),minimum=min(index),
       median=median(index),mean=mean(index),sd=sd(index),maximum=max(index)) |> tab()
stopifnot(!("operational_effectiveness_index" %in% names(data)),
          all(index >= 1 & index <= 5,na.rm=TRUE))
```

## Data preparation narrative and limitations

I kept the 32 questionnaire items, repaired labels, recoded nonresponses, and verified the reversals. Reliability, factor loadings, and item wording support only the employee proficiency index.

Missing borrowing-rate responses (16.4%) may affect comparisons. The case narrative describes 123 usable questionnaires, but this file contains 128 records. I retained all supplied records because there is no information identifying exclusions. Missing questions and the absence of respondent identifiers limit further checks and analysis of the case's broader objectives.

```{r}
          identical(map(roundtrip,~attr(.x,"labels")),map(data,~attr(.x,"labels"))))

       export="Case31_GM_cleaned.sav", verification="Reimport, values, labels, and dimensions passed") |> tab()
```
